title: Revant Himatsingka Quit a Rs 2 Crore US Job to Become the Food Pharmer
excerpt: Speaking at NDTV Yuva 2026, the food and health activist explained why 13 years in the US convinced him that India needs better health literacy around packaged food.
body:
• Revant Himatsingka, known as Food Pharmer, left a Rs 2 crore consulting job in the US and returned to India after 13 years abroad to raise awareness about packaged food.
  • He says misleading labels — like products marketed as "high protein" with just two or three grams of protein — drove his frustration with how packaged food is sold.
  • His core argument: "People in India are educated, but we are not health literate," distinguishing formal education from the ability to read and judge food labels.
  • At NDTV Yuva 2026 he also warned against energy drinks popular with children and teenagers, and said protein choice depends on the individual's body type and budget.

A high-protein claim with three grams of protein

Revant Himatsingka had spent 13 years in the United States building a career as a consultant to food companies. The work paid Rs 2 crore a year. But the more he studied how packaged food was marketed to consumers, the more frustrated he became — and he told the audience at NDTV Yuva 2026 that this frustration is what eventually pulled him back to India.

The food and health activist, better known to his millions of followers as Food Pharmer, said his doubts began in American grocery aisles. Products advertised as "high protein" would turn out to contain just two or three grams of protein per serving. He watched people leave the gym and drink a soft drink afterwards, convinced they had made a healthy choice. "So I thought, I have to do something about this. Why don't I leave the US and come back to India to raise awareness about this?" he said.

Context & Background

Himatsingka has built one of India's largest food-awareness followings by breaking down nutrition labels and questioning health claims on packaged products. His videos dissect ingredient lists and marketing slogans in plain language, and brands have responded — sometimes by reformulating products, sometimes by objecting. His move to return to India and work full-time on food awareness followed years of watching the same labeling tricks operate in the US, where he says consumers buy even more packaged food than Indians do.

The session at NDTV Yuva 2026, the network's youth summit, gave him a platform to explain the transition in his own words. His argument rests on a distinction he kept returning to: "People in India are educated, but we are not health literate. There is a big difference between being educated and being health literate."

Impact & Analysis

The distinction matters because India's packaged food market is expanding fast, and labels are getting more sophisticated while scrutiny stays thin. Health-literacy campaigns have historically focused on nutrition in the abstract — eat less sugar, read the label — while the marketing of ultra-processed food has moved toward precise-sounding claims like "high protein" or "no added sugar" that technically satisfy regulators but mislead shoppers. Himatsingka's approach — naming specific products and decoding claims one label at a time — has filled that gap in a way government advisories rarely do.

When asked which packaged products he would never buy, his first answer was energy drinks. He flagged their growing popularity among children and teenagers, saying an eight-year-old who wants to look cool will buy an energy drink the way an adult reaches for alcohol. Protein was the other major theme: Himatsingka, who has launched his own protein brand, said there are three types — whey, plant, and yeast — and declined to declare a winner. All three are fine, he said; the right choice depends on the individual's body type and what works for them, with plant and yeast proteins generally cheaper than whey.

Diaspora Angle

Himatsingka's arc will be familiar to many NRIs who have weighed a comfortable American career against work that feels more consequential back home. His specific diagnosis — that the US food system normalizes packaged food even more thoroughly than India's — adds a twist: returning was not about escaping a problem in India, but about bringing a sharper eye for one he had watched up close for 13 years. For diaspora families on both sides of the ocean, his message applies equally: the labels are designed by the same global playbook.

What's Next

Himatsingka continues to expand his food-awareness work in India, now paired with his own protein brand — a combination that invites both praise for walking the talk and scrutiny over conflicts of interest. Whether regulators follow his lead on stricter labeling rules remains the open question; India's front-of-pack labeling debate has stalled more than once. For now, his million-follower classroom remains the most effective food-labeling school in the country.
